statement: William is thinking of an integer between \(1\) and \(50\) inclusive. Victor can choose a positive integer \(m\) and ask William whether \(m\) divides William's number; William answers truthfully. Victor repeats until he determines the number. What is the minimum number of questions Victor needs to guarantee this?

There are \(20\) students in a class, each with exactly \(3\) close friends in the class. Five students initially buy concert tickets. If any student sees that at least \(2\) of their close friends have bought tickets, they also buy a ticket. Is it possible that eventually the entire class buys tickets? (Friendship is mutual.)

Let \(ABC\) be an acute triangle with altitudes \(AD\), \(BE\), \(CF\) meeting at \(H\). The circle through \(D\), \(E\), \(F\) meets \(AD\), \(BE\), \(CF\) again at \(X\), \(Y\), \(Z\) respectively. Prove that
\[\frac{AH}{DX} + \frac{BH}{EY} + \frac{CH}{FZ} \geq 3.\]

Let \(f(x)\) be a non-constant polynomial with integer coefficients with \(f(1) \neq 1\). For a positive integer \(n\), let \(\mathrm{divs}(n)\) be the set of positive divisors of \(n\). Call a positive integer \(m\) \(f\)-cool if there exists a positive integer \(n\) with \(f[\mathrm{divs}(m)] = \mathrm{divs}(n)\). Prove that for any such \(f\), there are finitely many \(f\)-cool integers.

A country with \(n\) cities has two-way roads between some pairs of cities. If the country is split into two parts in any way, at most \(kn\) roads go between the parts (where \(k\) is a fixed positive integer). What is the largest integer \(m\), in terms of \(n\) and \(k\), such that there is guaranteed to be a set of \(m\) cities with no two directly connected by a road?
